of statutory rules providing such absorption. However, as frequently reiterated, 
Uma Devi itself distinguishes between appointments that are “illegal” and those 
that are “irregular,” the latter being eligible for regularization if they meet 
certain conditions. More importantly, Uma Devi cannot serve as a shield to justify 
exploitative engagements persisting for years without the Employer undertaking 
legitimate recruitment. Given the record which shows no true contractor-based 
arrangement and a consistent need for permanent horticultural staff the alleged 
asserted ban on fresh recruitment, though real, cannot justify indefinite daily- 
wage status or continued unfair practices. 


॥उ It is manifest that the Appellant Workmen continuously rendered their services 
over several years, sometimes spanning more than a decade. Even if certain 
muster rolls were not produced in full, the Employer's failure to furnish such 
records—despite directions to do so—allows an adverse inference under well- 
established labour jurisprudence. Indian labour law strongly disfavors perpetual 
daily-wage or contractual engagements in circumstances where the work is 
permanent in nature. Morally and legally, workers who fulfil ongoing municipal 
requirements year after year cannot be dismissed summarily as dispensable, 
particularly in the absence of a genuine contractor agreement....” 


40. The principal issue which arises for consideration in the present case is whether the 
engagement of the workmen through contractors is genuine or merely a sham and camouflage devised to 
deny them the status and benefits of regular employees. Upon a careful appreciation of the pleadings, 
documentary evidence and the testimony of witnesses, this Tribunal is of the considered opinion that the 
contract labour arrangement in the present case is not genuine. Documentary evidence (Ex. DWI/I0) 
where A.L. Bhasin (DGM, GEO-]) certifying one of the claimants working with the management at the 
post of attendant for the last one year and other similar letter issued to Sh. Laxmi Dutt, Sh. Ram Kishan 
and letter addressed to Sh. Brijesh on 30.2.207 by Sh. Dinesh Kumar Sarraf, buttresses the fact that the 
arrangement between the management of ONGC and contractors are not genuine. This fact is also 
buttressed from the direct payments made to the workmen through cheques by the management of ONGC. 
The material on record clearly demonstrates that the workmen were working within the premises of the 
Management and were subject to its direct control and supervision. The attendance records, duty rosters, 
identity cards, gate passes and shift reports (४5.9४४५७४।/5) placed on record unmistakably establish that the 
day-to-day functioning of the workmen was regulated by the officials of the Management. The 
Management witness, on the other hand, has admitted lack of personal knowledge regarding crucial aspects 
of supervision and engagement and has failed to explain the role of the contractors in any meaningful 
manner. This clearly indicates that the real and effective control over the workmen was exercised by the 
Management. 


4\. Further, the evidence also points towards the existence of economic control with the 
Management. It has come on record that in certain instances, the Management had directly made payments 
to the workmen when the contractors defaulted. The Management has failed to produce cogent and reliable 
evidence to establish that the contractors had independent financial control over the workmen or that the 
wages were exclusively paid by them in a structured and autonomous manner. The absence of proper wage 
records and supporting documents further weakens the stand of the Management. An equally significant 
circumstance is the admitted position that while the contractors were changed from time to time, the 
workmen continued to work uninterruptedly for several years, in many cases extending over decades. Such 
continuity of the same set of workmen, despite change of contractors, clearly establishes that the 
contractors were merely intermediaries or name-lenders and that the arrangement was a device to avoid 
statutory obligations. 


42. The nature of duties performed by the workmen further fortifies this conclusion. The workmen 
have been engaged in activities such as security services, clerical work, maintenance and other allied 
functions, all of which are essential and indispensable to the day-to-day functioning of the establishment. 
These are not intermittent or seasonal activities but are of a continuous and perennial nature. The long 
duration of service rendered by the workmen, coupled with the nature of duties performed, leaves no 
manner of doubt that the work is permanent in character. Indeed, the evidence on record clearly establishes 


[भाग ]---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जुलाई , 2026/ आषाढ 20, 948 6867 


that the services rendered by the workmen are so vital to the functioning of the establishment that their 
removal would seriously disrupt, if not completely paralyze, the operations of the Management. 


43. Applying the well-settled legal tests, this Court finds that both the Integration Test and the 
Continuity of Service Test stand fully satisfied in the present case. The workmen are fully integrated into 
the organizational framework of the Management, performing functions which are integral to its 
operations. Their long and uninterrupted service, notwithstanding the change of contractors, clearly 
establishes continuity of employment in substance. These factors cumulatively lead to the irresistible 
conclusion that the relationship between the parties is that of employer and employee, notwithstanding the 
ostensible contractual arrangement. 


44. The workmen have also successfully demonstrated that they have been performing duties 
similar to those performed by regular employees of the Management, yet they have been paid substantially 
lesser wages and denied corresponding benefits. The Management has failed to establish any rational basis 
for such disparity. In these circumstances, the constitutional principle of “equal pay for equal work” is 
clearly attracted. The denial of parity in wages and service benefits amounts to unfair labour practice and 
cannot be sustained. 


45. Insofar as the question of regularization is concerned, the objection of the Management based 
on the principle against backdoor entry is misplaced in the facts of the present case. The workmen have not 
secured employment through any fraudulent or illegal means; rather, they have been continuously engaged 
for long years under the direct control and supervision of the Management. The contract labour system 
having been found to be sham, the workmen cannot be denied the benefit of regularization on the ground of 
procedural irregularities. The long and continuous service rendered by them in perennial and essential 
activities confers upon them a legitimate right to be treated as regular employees. Denial of such status 
would amount to perpetuation of unfair labour practice. Consequently, the action of the Management in 
denying regularization and consequential benefits to the workmen is held to be unjust, unfair and illegal. 


Relief 


In view of the discussion made herein above, the workmen’s services except those who had left the 
services of the management/respondent, are entitled to be regularized along with all consequential benefits 
since their initial date of appointment. The workmen who retired during the pendency of the proceedings 
are also entitled for consequential benefits arising out of their regularization. The workmen who had 
expired during pendency of this claim petition, are also entitled for regularization, and their legal heirs be 
given benefits of regularization. The award shall be complied with by the management within two months 
from the date of notification of this award. Award is passed accordingly. A copy of this award be sent to 
the appropriate government for notification under section 7 of the I.D Act. The file is consigned to record 
room.

through a special power of attorney to undertake work on its behalf, the relationship of employer and 
employee was established. Relying upon the said judgment, the claimant contended that ४५७।], in his

4th-5th Floor, 29, Barakhamba Road, Connaught Place, and further admitted having received the notice

admission of ०७] that upon receipt of technical complaints, employees of IGL used to visit the houses of

It was further pointed out that जि] admitted the documents marked as ‘C’ (pages 0] to 36), 
consisting photocopies of GI removal/modification forms containing the signatures of the claimant as well 
as the concerned customers. The claimant further highlighted the admission of ५७] that no document

EPF Office, Lucknow, pertaining to May, 2007. He further admitted that no document had been filed to 
establish that during the relevant period the claimant was working under the said contractor. 


It is a well-settled principle of law that the onus to prove the relationship of employer and 
employee rests upon the claimant. His appointment letter, wage slip and the mode of payment are essential 
ingredients for establishing the relationship. However, it cannot be said that in the absence of these 
documents, the relationship of employer and employee cannot be established from the material available 
on record. It can be established by circumstantial evidence, ancillary evidence or secondary evidence. 


Here, the ४५७४] admitted that the document marked as ‘C’ (pages 0 to 36) consisting photocopies 
of GI removal/modification form containing the signatures of the claimant as well as the concerned 
customers. Here, the management has failed to produce any documentary evidence in rebuttal that at the 
relevant time, it had entered into contract with M/s. Unitech Ltd. for the above said period and the wages 
bills had been paid to the contractor of the claimant. 


The labour license obtained by the CLRA Act has nothing to do with the present matter. Even the 
record produced by the management from the office of EPFO, Lucknow pertaining to May, 2007 while the 
claimant alleged that his services were terminated by the management in the year 2006 itself. 


Non-production of the contract entered by management with M/s. Unitech Ltd. as alleged of the 
relevant period has established that the claimant was the employee of the management. Further, non- 
production of the record coupled with the fact that the management has not called witnesses from M/s. 
Unitech Ltd. to establish that the claimant was employed by M/s. Unitech Ltd. at the premises of the 
management, the claimant has, therefore, proved that it was an employee of the management of I.G.L., and 
the issue no. | goes in favour of the claimant and against the management. 


Coming to issue no. 2, Section 2(00) defines the term ‘retrenchment’ while section 25F of the Act 
has set out the conditions to be complied by an employer before retrenching a workman. Definition of 
section 2(00) and section 25F of Act are as follows: 


[(00) “retrenchment” means the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for 
any reason whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action, 
but does not include— 


(a) voluntary retirement of the workman; or 


(b) retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of 
employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that 
behalf; or 


[(bb) termination of the service of the workman as a result of the non-renewal of the contract of 
employment between the employer and the workman concerned on its expiry or of such contract 
being terminated under a stipulation in that behalf contained therein; or] ( 


c) termination of the service of a workman on the ground of continued ill-health;] 


25F. Conditions precedent to retrenchment of workmen: No workman employed in any industry 
who has been in continuous service for not less than one year under an employer shall be 
retrenched by that employer until- 


6872 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : JULY ], 2026/ ASHADHA 20, 948 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


(a) the workman has been given one month’s notice in writing indicating the reasons for 
retrenchment and the period of notice has expired, or the workman has been paid in lieu of 
such notice, wages for the period of the notice; 


(b) the workman has been paid, at the time of retrenchment, compensation which shall be 
equivalent to fifteen days' average pay 2 [for every completed year of continuous service] or any 
part thereof in excess of six months; and 


(c) notice in the prescribed manner is served on the appropriate Government 3 [or such 
authority as may be specified by the appropriate Government by notification in the Official 
Gazette]. 


The said section itself created four exceptions where the termination of services of the claimant 
does not come within the definition of ‘retrenchment’. The section itself creates a bar upon the 
retrenchment when the services were terminated by way of punishment. 


From the pleadings and evidence placed on record, it stands established that the claimant had been 
working continuously with the management and that his services were terminated on 22.09.2006 by not 
assigning him any further duty. The management has failed to place on record any material to show that 
the claimant’s services were terminated for any misconduct or under any exception carved out under 
Section 2(00) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947. The termination of the claimant, therefore, squarely 
falls within the definition of “retrenchment” as provided under Section 2(00) of the Act. 


If the management intended to retrench the claimant, it was required to comply with the mandatory 
provisions of Section 25F of the Act by giving one month’s prior notice or wages in lieu thereof. 
Additionally, the management was also required to pay retrenchment compensation equivalent to 5 days’ 
average pay for every completed year of continuous service. 


However, there is nothing on record to show that prior to terminating the services of the claimant, 
the management had complied with the mandatory provisions of Section 25F of the Act by giving one 
month’s notice or wages in lieu of notice and by paying retrenchment compensation to the claimant at the 
time of termination. Non-compliance of the mandatory conditions prescribed under Section 25F renders 
the retrenchment illegal and unjustified. Accordingly, the termination of the services of the claimant is held 
to be illegal and unjustified. 


Now, the question that arises is with regard to the relief to which the claimant is entitled to. As a 
general rule, where termination is declared illegal, the appropriate relief is reinstatement with full back 
wages. However, it has been held by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India in Employers, Management of 
central P & D Inst. Ltd. vs. Union of India & Another, AIR 2005 Supreme Court 633 that it is not 
always mandatory to order reinstatement even where the termination is held illegal and compensation can 
be granted instead by the industrial adjudicator. Similar views were expressed by the Hon’ble High Court 
of Delhi in Indian Hydraulic Industries Pvt. Ltd. vs. Kishan Devi and Bhagwati Devi & Ors., wherein it 
was held that even if the termination is found to be illegal, the relief of reinstatement with full back wages 
need not be granted automatically and the relief may be moulded according to the facts and circumstances 
of each case, including grant of compensation in lieu of reinstatement and back wages. The same principle 
has been reiterated by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation 
vs. Mahadeo Krishna Naik (2025 (INSC) 28), wherein it was held that reinstatement with full back 
wages is not an automatic relief and, in appropriate cases, lump sum compensation may be a more suitable 
relief. 


Considering the facts and circumstances of the present case and prolonged litigation faced by the 
claimant, lump sum compensation of Rs. 5,00,000/- (Rupees Five Lakhs Only) is considered an 
appropriate relief in lieu of reinstatement. Accordingly, a lump sum compensation of Rs. 5,00,000/- 
(Rupees Five Lakhs Only) is awarded to the claimant in lieu of reinstatement and back wages. The 
management is directed to pay the said amount within two months from the date of publication of this 
Award, failing which the amount shall carry interest @ 8% per annum from the date of Award till its 
realization.

the Industrial Disputes Act, 947. The file is consigned to the Record Room.

7. Admittedly the concerned workmen who are about 300 in numbers were retrenched by the 
management of M/s. GOCL by sending them notice (Exhibit W-8, Exhibit M-l, Exhibit M-2 and 
Exhibit M-3 Series) and on its perusal it is crystal clear that the notices to the concerned employees as 
well as information to the Secretary Govt. of India of Ministry of Labour, New Delhi was sent under 
clause (c) of Section 25F of I.D. Act 947 and Form-P and Rules 76 of Industrial Dispute Rules 957 
whereas admittedly the management is covered under chapter V-B and accordingly the management was 
under legal obligation by virtue of Section 25 N of ILD. Act, 947 to send 3 months notice in writing to 
the concerned workmen indicating the reasons and the notice must have been sent under prescribed 
Form —“P(A)” under Rules 76-A of the Industrial Dispute Rules 957 for retrenchment but the 
management has violated this mandatory provisions and therefore, the notices for retrenchment sent by 
the management under clause (c) of Section 25F of the I.D. Act, !947 and Form-P of the I.D. Rules 
957 are illegal making the retrenchment invalid and void ab-initio and so in such circumstances it shall 
be deemed that the concerned workmen have not been issued any notice prior to their retrenchment 
which is mandatory and therefore, they are entitled to 3 months notice pay as well as the retrenchment 
benefit accordingly. 


8. Thus on the basis of above discussions of evidence this Tribunal finds and holds that the actions 
of the management of M/s. GOCL (The Contractor) is not justified for denying the payment of 3 months 
notice pay and retrenchment benefit to 226 retrenched workmen whose names were submitted before 
ALC (C) Chaibasa at conciliation stage and the management is directed accordingly to make payment of

20. Issue (4i) whether non implementation of equal pay for equal work is justified. 


The principal of “Equal pay for Equal work” is a constitutional goal. In the case of State of Punjab 
& ors. -vrs- Jagjit Singh (207) ISCC 48, the Hon’ble Supreme Court held that temporary employees are 
entitled to wages at per with the minimum of the pay scale of regular employees, discharging the same 
duties. 


2: The management’s witness herself (0॥५७०-]) admitted in cross examination that the claimants have 
been working as casual workers for 25/26 years. The management’s contention that the roles, 
responsibilities and accountability of regular employee are entirely different from contingent workers is 
bare assertion unsupported by evidence. 


22: The evidence in the present case clearly established that the 4 claimants have performing duties 
identical to those of regular Grade-I[V employees under the same supervisory control on a perennial and 
full time basis. The management itself has provided the claimants with certain facilities (annual leave, 
yearly bonus, overtime allowance, limited medical benefits) all of which are attributes of regular 
employment. No material distinction regarding qualification, nature of work, workload or responsibility 
has been shown by the management. 


23. In the above, replying the judgement of the Apex Court in State of Punjab vs. Jagjit Singh & Ors. 
(Supra) and following the constitutional principle enshrined in Article 39(d) read with Articles l4 and 6 
of the Constitution of India, management is hereby directed to intend the benefit of ‘Equal pay for Equal 
work’ to the concerned workmen and to pay wages at par with regular Grade IV employees from the date 
they become entitled to. 


24. Accordingly, the Management of ONGC Ltd., Tripura Asset, Agartala is hereby directed to 
consider the cases of the surviving claimants for regularization/absorption in Group-D (Grade IV) posts on 
priority basis in the next arising vacancies, in compliance with the MRPR-80 and the direction of the

The facts of the case in a narrow compass are as under :- 


According to second party union, as per its Statement of Claim (Exh. U-5), that first party Army Public 
School, BEG & Centre, Khadki, Pune, is an educational institution under the control of its 
management. Wherein about 60-70 workers are employed and the entire supervision and 
administration vests with the management. Despite, the first party school has not framed any 
independent service rules governing the service conditions of the concerned workers. Apart, the 
concermed workers, whose details are set out in Annexure “A”, were appointed after due process and 
had rendered long, continuous and satisfactory service with clean and unblemished service record. 
Despite they were not extended legal wages and statutory benefits such as leave, bonus and other 
service entitlements. 


Furthermore, the first party school, with a view to deprive the workers of their legitimate rights, 
introduced M/s. MGA Services as a contractor and attempted to create a sham and bogus arrangement. 
Around January 205, the workers were suddenly informed that, they would no longer be treated as 
employees of its school, but as contract labour, without issuing any written order or following due 
process. Apart the workers had completed more than 240 days of continuous service in each year. 
However, their services came to be terminated without issuing notice, notice pay or retrenchment 
compensation. Thus, the termination was effected arbitrarily and in violation of the principles of 
natural justice. Because no seniority list was prepared or published and the mandatory procedure under 
law was not followed. On the contrary, junior employees were retained in service. 


Moreover, when the workers approached first party school for reinstatement, they were denied 
employment and threatened or prevented from resuming duties and their repeated representations were 
not considered. Upon which, the dispute was raised before the Conciliation Authority. However, due to 
the adamant and non-cooperative attitude of first party school, no amicable settlement could be arrived 
at and consequently, the matter came to be referred for adjudication. Therefore, second party union 
prayed that, the concerned employees as mentioned in Annexure-A may be reinstated at their original 
post in the establishment of first party school with continuity of service and full back wages and 
consequential benefits w. e. f. 06.02.20I5. 


Upon, the first party School has appeared and filed its written statement at Exh. C-6 and opposed the 
claim of the second party union as untenable and not maintainable in law. Further, the second party 
union has no locus standi to raise the present dispute. Wherein, no employer-employee relationship 
exists between its school and the employees, whose names are mentioned in Annexure “A”, as they 
were never appointed nor borne on its rolls. Rather, the said employees were engaged, if at all, through 
an independent contractor, namely M/s. MGA Services, Moreover, compliance of statutory provisions 
such as provident fund does not establish employer—employee relationship. Furthermore, its school, 
being an educational institution, is stated to be outside the purview of “industry” under the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 947.

Heard. Wherein, Representative for second party in addition to written notes of argument at Exh.U-62 
also argued that, the concerned were direct employees of the of the first party school and were

adopted only to deprive the the concerned employees of their legitimate statutory rights. The 
termination of services of them, despite completion of more than 240 days of continuous service, was 
effected without notice, notice pay, or retrenchment compensation and in clear violation of principles 
of natural justice and mandatory provisions of law. Further, no seniority list was maintained and junior

question of illegal termination by the first Party does not arise. Thus, the second party union has no 
locus standi, and therefore, the reference deserves to be rejected. Besides, the Representative for first 
party also relied upon the reported judgment our Hon’ble High Court in the matters of P.G. 
Virgincar & Company V/s. S.V. Nevagi, Presiding Officer, Educational Tribunal Government of 
Goa & Ors. 995(2) Bom.C.R. 304 and Ramasare Yadav V/s. Manikgarh Cement Factory, 200

. AS TO ISSUE NO. TO 3:- Heard. Having regards to the submissions made by Representatives for 


both the parties and having considered oral evidence of parties. Wherein Smt. Shobha Gaikwad, Smt. 
Mangal Bhande, Smt. Nirmala Bhise, Smt. Savita Waghmare, and Smt. Premkumari Pradhan, at Exh. 
U-I5, Exh. U-7, Exh. U-9, Exh. U-2l, Exh. U-48, Exh. U-49 and Exh. U-50, respectively in their

documentary proof to establish employer—employee relationship with the first party school. Similarly, 
they admitted that, their names were reflected in EPF records of M/s. MGA Services and not of the first 
party school. Moreover, they admitted that, they were not regular employees of the first party school 
and were working on daily wages. Besides, they admitted that, they were unaware as to who was 
supervising or paying their wages and had no knowledge of the contractual arrangement between the 
first party school and M/s. MGA Services. Apart, they admitted that, they have not filed any agreement 
or document showing direct employment with the first party school. Likewise, they admitted that, they 
had not received salary slips and wages were paid in cash. Significantly, they admitted that, they had 
no documentary proof of their date of birth, appointment or continuity of service. Further, they 
admitted that, they have not worked with the concerned union and were unaware how the said union 
represents their case. Moreover, they admitted that, they have not made efforts to secure alternate 
employment and some of them stated that they are not in need of employment. Similarly, they admitted 
that, the first party school is situated in an Army area and access requires gate pass, however, they were

no material to substantiate their claim of direct employment. 


3. In the rebuttal, the witness of the first party, Shri Girishchandra Ramdata Mathani, at Exh. C-25, in his 
cross-examination admitted that, there was no direct connection between the first party school and the 
concerned employees. Moreover, he stated that, he had applied for tender (Exh. C-23) with first party 
school. Similarly, he denied the suggestion that, any false documents were created or he had deposed 
falsely. Further, he denied that, he had not received payment of bills. Likewise, he denied any 
allegation of collusion with the first party school. Thus except this, nothing material or fruitful could be 
extracted from his mouth during the course of cross-examination. 


4. Likewise, the another witness of the first party, Smt. Arti Sharma, in her cross-examination below Exh. 
C-87 admitted that, she took charge as Officiating Principal only on !4.09.20l4 and became regular 
Principal in February 205 and had no knowledge whether the concerned employees were working in 
the first party school prior to 204. Significantly, she admitted that, the provident fund documents 
shown to her do not mention the name of the first party School. Moreover, she expressed lack of 
knowledge about the provident fund slips and various documents produced by the second party, 
including annual reports and other records. Further, she admitted that, though certain documents 
reflected names of the concerned employees, she had no knowledge about the same. Likewise, she 
admitted that, the copy of the tender is not filed on record, and all procedures relating to the contractor 
were carried out prior to her joining. Besides, she admitted that, except vouchers and bills at Exh. C- 
23, no cheque or bank statement is filed to show payment to the contractor. Further she denied the 
suggestion that, the members of the second party union were employees of the first party school and 
clarified that, their services were terminated by the contractor, M/s. MGA Services, and not by the First 
Party School. Moreover, she categorically denied that, the contractor was bogus or that there was any 
collusion between the first party school and the contractor. 


5. Upon careful appreciation of oral evidence of concerned employees, it is evident that, they have failed 
to establish the essential ingredient of employer—employee relationship with the first party school, as 
they have admittedly not produced any appointment letters, salary slips or any documentary proof in 
that regard. Besides, their own admissions clearly show that, their names were reflected in EPF records 
of M/s. MGA Services and they were working on daily wages without any knowledge of supervision or 
control by the first party school. Moreover, their admissions regarding absence of documentary proof, 
ignorance about contractual arrangement, and lack of connection with the union further weaken their 
claim. On the contrary, the evidence of the first Party witnesses, namely Shri Girishchandra Mathani 
and Smt. Arti Sharma, supports the case of the first party that, the concerned employees were engaged 
through contractor M/s. MGA Services and that there was no direct relationship with the First Party 
School. Thus, from the oral evidence on record, it clearly emerges that, the concerned workers were not 
the employees of the first party school. 


6. Besides, it is seen from the documentary evidence produced by the first party at Exh. C-35 to Exh. C- 
37 that, the first party school had followed a due and lawful tender process by publishing a tender 
notice in newspaper and thereafter awarding the contract to M/s. MGA Services vide Supply Order 
dated 02/09/204 (Exh. C-37). Further, from the documents at Exh. C-38 to Exh. C-73, consisting of 
monthly bills, vouchers and receipts for the period September 20l4 to August 205, it clearly 
establishes that, the first party school had made payments only to the contractor, M/s. MGA Services 
and not to the concerned employees. Besides, the Bank Statements produced at Exh. C-96 corroborate 
the said payments and further strengthen the existence of a principal—contractor relationship between 
the first Party school and M/s. MGA Services. Moreover, the termination letter at Exh. C-74 clearly 
shows that, the services of the concerned workers were terminated by M/s. MGA Services and not by 
the first party school. Apart from this, the muster roll and wage register at Exh. C-82 as well as 
EPF/PPF records at Exh. C-83 demonstrate that, the concerned employees were engaged by and 
received wages and statutory benefits from M/s. MGA Services. 


7. So far as the documents filed by the concerned employees, viz. EPF statements, identity cards, school 
magazines and muster rolls at Exh. U-27, U-28, U-36 (colly), U-43 (colly), U-58 (colly), U-58A (colly) 
and other allied documents are concerned, the same are of no assistance to the case of the second party, 
because they do not establish any employer—employee relationship with the First Party School. Firstly,

the EPF statements only reflect contribution through M/s. MGA Services and do not mention the First 
Party School as employer. Secondly, the identity cards are merely for entry or identification purposes 
and do not confer any status of employment. Besides, the school magazines and photographs are not 
proof of employment. Moreover, the muster rolls relied upon are not proved in accordance with law 
and do not connect the concerned employees with the First Party School. Hence, the said documents 
are insufficient and unreliable to prove the claim of direct employment with the first party. 


. Upon careful appreciation of the entire oral as well as documentary evidence on record, I am of the 


considered opinion that, the second party union has failed to establish the existence of employer— 
employee relationship between the First Party School and the employees mentioned in Annexure “A”. 
Because it is evident from the consistent admissions of the concerned employees, coupled with the 
absence of any appointment orders, salary records or cogent documentary evidence, which clearly 
negate their claim of direct employment with the First Party. Moreover, the documentary evidence 
produced by the first party, particularly the tender documents, bills, vouchers, bank statements and the 
termination letter, conclusively establishes that, the services of the concerned employees were 
outsourced to M/s. MGA Services and they were engaged, paid and terminated by the said contractor. 
Therefore, I am further of the opinion that, the present reference is not maintainable in law as there 
exists no relationship of employer and employee between the First party school and the concerned 
employees. 


. Apart it is clear by the reported judgment of our Hon’ble High Court in the matter of P.G. Virgincar 


& Company (supra) as referred by first party that, if the Union has no locus standi, then there is no 
valid industrial dispute, and consequently, the reference and the award are not maintainable in law. In 
the present matter also, the second party union has failed to establish its locus standi, as the concerned 
employees themselves have admitted lack of any employer—employee relationship with the first party 
School and have not produced any authorization or cogent material to show that, the Union is 
competent to espouse their cause. Similarly it is clear by another reported judgment of our Hon’ble 
High Court in the matter of Ramasare Yadav (supra) as relied on by the first party that, if a worker 
fails to prove employer—employee relationship and the evidence shows he was working through a 
contractor, the claim must fail. In the present case, since the employees admitted lack of proof and 
records show they were engaged by M/s. MGA Services, there is no direct relationship with the first 
party. So far as the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India in Special Leave to Appeal (C) 
No. 3609 of 206 (arising out of the impugned final judgment and order dated 29.0.205 in LPA 
No. 227/205 passed by the Hon’ble High Court of Delhi at New Delhi) in the matter of Army 
Welfare Education Society & Anr. (supra) is concerned, as relied upon by the second party, since the 
facts of the said case are clearly distinguishable from the facts of the present case. Hence, the ratio laid 
down therein is not applicable to the present matter. 


Consequently, in the light of above factual and legal matrix, I am of the opinion that, second party 
union has miserably failed to prove that, services of employees as mentioned in Annexure-A were 
illegally terminated by first party school on 06.02.205. Accordingly, they are not entitled to the relief 
of reinstatement with continuity of service and full back wages w.e.f. 06.02.20l5 alongwith 
consequential reliefs. As a result thereof, Issue No.| to 3 are answered in the negative.

Central Government vide Notification No.L-420]/46/2020-IR(DU), dated 06.08.2020, under 
clause (d) of sub-section (l) and subsection 2(A) of Section l0 of the Industrial Disputes Acct, 
947(hereinafter called the Act), has referred the following Industrial dispute for adjudication to this 
Tribunal:- 


“Whether the demand of the Centre of Indian Trade Union (CITU), Dehradun vide 
letter dated .09.209 to the management of Forest Research Institute, Dehradun to 
regularize the contract workers (37+68=05 workers) is proper, legal and justified? If 
yes, what relief the claimant is entitled to and what directions, if any, are necessary in 
the matter? 


l. All the parties were served with notices. The applicant/claimant appeared and filed its claim 
statement on 05.0.2020 maintaining therein that the present claim has been filed through State Secretary 
of Centre of Indian Trade Union (CITU) Uttrakhand and claimant has espoused the cause of 05 workers 
of the respondent no.|. It is maintained that workers are working with the respondent no.! from almost last 
5 years, who have not only been appointed by the authorities of respondent no.l, but their work is also 
being monitored and controlled by the respondent no.!. However, respondent no.] is disbursing the salary 
of the aforesaid workers through contractors. Through letter dated .06.209, claimant raised industrial 
dispute for regularization of services of the aforesaid workmen and in addition to that, they have also raised 
many other question regarding the harassment and illegality done by the respondent no.!. Even thereafter, 
they have not been regularized. Workmen had worked for more than 240 days in terms of Act in every 
calendar year but they fear termination of services.

2. It is further maintained that on .08.2020, fresh advertisements were issued by the FRI 
(respondent no.!) for various posts despite of the fact that the matter has already been referred to the 
Industrial Tribunal for its disposal. There is permanent requirement of staff with the respondent no.! and 
there are permanent posts. Workmen, who are contractual employees, have been working for almost 5 to 
20 years, but they have not been regularized. Respondent no.! had engaged the workmen on contractual 
basis opposing the public policy and is exploiting the workmen, which is unfair labour practice. Applicants 
are governed by the Model Standing Order, which are having statutory force and respondent no.! is bound 
by the said standing orders and as per Clause 3(b), six categories stated in those standing orders are of 
permanent status. So the proposed action of respondent no.| by advertising posts is illegal, contrary to 
Section 23 of the Indian Contract Act and amounts to unfair labour practice. Nature of duties and hours of 
working of all the contractual workmen is identical and at par with regular employees. The workmen had 
filed the application under Section 33 of the Act for not filling up the different posts as mentioned in 
advertisement dated .08.2020 and 09.2.2022. However, application of the workmen was dismissed by 
the Court of Sh. J K Tripathi, the then Presiding Officer, CGIT-II, Chandigarh vide its order dated 
05.0!.2023. Against the said order, applicants have gone in appeal before the Hon'ble Uttrakhand High 
Court at Nainital and vide order dated 2!.02.2023 interim order providing that till next date of listing, 
engagement of the members of petitioner trade union shall not be discontinued. The same order was 
reaffirmed vide order dated 04.06.2024 in the writ petition. Vide order dated 20.06.2025, the stay was 
granted for another six months. It is maintained by the workmen that since fresh advertisement has been 
issued by the respondent no.| for filling up the various posts was in pursuance thereof, applicants have also 
applied for the same. However, for the posts in question, although the workers have applied for the same 
through online, but their applications were not considered as there was no provision for regularization in 
the age and qualification for contractual workmen. Workmen met respondent no.l, however it shows its 
inability to appoint workmen. Alleged contract and contractual appointment is a sham show and 
exploitation of the workmen and also unfair labour practice as prescribed in 5th Schedule in Item No.0 of 
the Act. 


3५ Respondent no.! wants to take benefit of Section 2(00)(bb) of the Act, wherein it is provided that 
various provisions of the Act are not applicable in case the appointment is for the fixed terms. But in this 
case, work of the workmen is perennial in nature and false plea being taken by the respondent no. . 


4. It is maintained that respondent no.| is engaging various contractors for different period, however, 
service is being taken from the workmen by the respondent no.! continuously and the said contractual 
agreements with the various contractors are sham transactions and in violation of the principle of natural 
justice, provisions of Constitution and in violation of laws laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court and 
other Hon'ble High Courts in various judgments, wherein it is provided that if there is sham contract, then 
workmen should be treated as employee of the principle employer. Hence, it is maintained that all the 
workmen be regularized from the date of reference along with all consequential benefits with further 
damage of Rs.5 Crore on account of unfair labour practice. 


dD. Respondent no.| filed written statement thereof maintaining therein that there is no contract 
between the workmen and respondent no.| directly or indirectly. The workmen are the employees of the 
service providers. Tenders were invited from time to time from service providers and contract was given to 
the lowest tenderer for providing employees with the respondent no.l. The workmen, who are members of 
applicant/claimant, have not received any letter of appointment from respondent no.l. There is no privity 
of contract between workmen and principle employer. The workers are under direct control and 
supervision of service providers i.e. respondent no.2 to 5. The workmen were deployed for specific task 
according to the instructions of the service providers and therefore, the workmen cannot be treated as 
regular employees of respondent no.l. The applicability of constitutional scheme of public employment 
applicable to the union government and instrumentalities of state come within the purview of Article 2 of 
the constitution of India. The power of a state as an employer is more limited than that of private employer 
in as much as it is subjected to constitutional limitations and cannot be exercised arbitrarily, public 
employment in a sovereign socialist secular democratic republic has to be as a set down by the constitution 
and the laws made there under. Various contracts have been issued between the respondent no.! and 
service providers, which are part of the written statement and as per the various agreement executed 
between service providers and respondent no.|, contractors shall be responsible for providing of personnel 
for the purpose mentioned in the agreements, who would in direct control or supervision of contractors. 
Even in case of any omission or commission or misconduct or indiscipline by any workman, concerned

the respondent no.| directly appointed the daily wage workers working under the CPWD by adjusting them 
on the same posts in its employment. Attendance was marked in office of respondent no.] and wages were 
paid by respondent no.l. So workmen worked directly with respondent no.l up to 08.2.200] as is clear

respondent no.! for filing up various permanent posts with it, but no relaxation in service was given to the 
claimant to enable them to get regular appointment, which is also unfair labour practice. This fact has been

by such unfair labour practice. However, the victims of unfair labour practice of the employer deserve 
freedom of permanency where facts and circumstanced demand in the canvas of Casterbe. 


67. It is pertinent to mention that the judgment of Casterbe dealt with MRTU & PULP Act enacted by 
the State of Maharashtra but the provisions of unfair labour practice are identical to Entry 0 of the 5th 
Schedule to the Industrial Disputes Act, 947. Entry l0 is a statutory protection against individual 
discrimination and exploitation provided the discrimination continues ‘for years’. It would follow that short 
duration of employment is per se not violative of Entry 0 of the Act and length of employment becomes 
relevant consideration to examine unfair labour practice issues. In Umadevi the Constitution Bench 
protected regularization done but those appointments which were not sub-judice could not be reopened. In 
terms of Umadevi, a distinction will have to be kept in mind between irregular appointments and illegal 
ones in view of the directions in para 44 to para 46, and thus a distinction would also have to be kept in 
mind between regularization and giving permanency. 


68. Though Casterbe is a case arising out of industrial adjudication on a complaint made by the Union 
of workers that the affected employees were engaged by the Corporation as casual labourers for cleaning 
the buses between 98-985 but the contested issue before the labour tribunal was whether the workers 
could be granted the status of permanency on par with other permanent cleaners. The Industrial Court, 
Bombay held that the complaint regarding unfair labour practice against the Corporation under Item 6 of 
Schedule IV was not maintainable. However, the complaints were maintainable in respect of the unfair 
labour practice under items 5, 9 and l0. A finding was returned that unfair labour practice has been 
committed under items 5 and 9 of schedule IV, Section 30 of the Maharashtra State Act empowers the 
Industrial and the Labour Courts to decide on any person named in the complaint if he has engaged in or is 
engaging in any unfair labour practice. It may in its order give declarations and directions accordingly. 
Items 5, 6 and 9 of Schedule IV to the MRTU & PULP Acts need to be seen. They read:- 


“5. To show favouritism or partiality to one set of workers, regardless of merits. 


. To employ employees as “badlis”, casuals or temporaries and to continue them as such for years, with 
the object of depriving them of the status and privileges of permanent employees. 


9. Failure to inplement award, settlement or agreement.” 


69. Item 6 of Schedule IV is identical to Entry 0 of the 5" Schedule to the Central Act and, therefore, 
would suffer common interpretation. The expression “unfair labour practice” in Section 2(ra) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 947 is defined to mean any of the practices specified in the 57 Schedule. It may 
be noted that the Industrial Disputes Act, !947 does not contain a provision like Section 30 of the MRTU 
& PULP Act in Maharashtra. Unfair labour practice in the Central Act is placed in Chapter VC. Section 
25T and 25U deal with prohibition and penalty for committing unfair labour practice. Thus, there is a 


[भाग ए---खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : जुलाई I], 2026/ आषाढ 20, 948 692] 


complete statutory prohibition against an employer, workmen or trade union against committing an unfair 
labour practice. Though the consequences of violating the provisions of Section 25T of the Industrial 
Disputes Act is punishment with imprisonment but that does not mean that the Labour Court is barred to 
exercise its powers of making declarations and issuing directions where a prima facie case is made out of 
violation of the law. In fact, Entry 0 of the 57 schedule is a rule against exploitation. It is a rule against 
modern day slavery and against unfair domination. Unfair labour practice is akin to unfair discrimination. 
They both belong to the same family. Entry |0 of the Central Act and Entry 6 of the Maharashtra Act pre- 
supposes that a body of workers under the same employer and doing the same thing are permanent while 
others not. Unfair labour practice would thus fall in the same cluster of grounds of challenge of 
administrative action as those when the Writ Court deals with in cases of malafides, malice in law, malice 
in fact, bias, colourable exercise or power or abuse of authority and so on and so forth. Merely because the 
Central Act does not contain specific provisions such as those in MRTU & PULP Act and of Section 30 
thereof, it would not denude this Tribunal to remove unfair discrimination whenever found in the light of 
discussion of Casterbe case.

8. So far as Kirlosker Brothers Ltd. Vs. Ramcharan and others (2022 INSC 7255) relied upon by 


the AR for respondent no.| is concerned, facts and circumstances of this case are distinguishable. In the

82. The next question for consideration is with respect to the unfair labour practice and its 
consequences. It is a settled law that in order to constitute an unfair labour practice under Section 2(ra) read 
with Item 0 of the Vth Schedule of the ID Act, the employer should be engaging workmen as temporary 
or casual and continuing them for years with the object of depriving them of the benefits payable to regular 
workmen. The Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Durgapur Casual Workers Union and others V/s 
Food Corporation of India, Civil Appeal ५०. 7/0856 of 20/4, dated 0०, /2, 20/4, has held that continued 
casualisation of service of workman amounts to unfair labour practice. In this case, the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court has observed that management was rightly directed by the Tribunal to absorb the workman. In the 
case of The workmen of Bhurkunda Colliery of M/s Central Coalfields Ltd. Vs. The Management of 

Bhurkunda Colliery of M/s Central Coalfields Ltd., arising out of Civil Appeal १०. /600 of 2005 dated 
22.07/. 2006, the Hon’ble Supreme Court dealing with the casual labour and work charged employees has 
held that if a casual labours work continuously of 2-3 years regular need of the service is presumed. Rule 
of Law is to the extent and action must be with Article !4 and 6 of the Constitution. So far as the case in 
hand is concerned, it is a proven fact that workmen are rendering their services to the establishment even 
on contract basis for more than |5 years. Thus, it can be clearly infer that there is sufficient work with the 
establishment regarding activities of respondent no.l, for which they are engaging these workmen 
continuously. 


83. Undoubtedly, the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act are made for the settlement of Industrial 
Disputes and for certain other provisions mentioned therein. The Act prohibits unfair labour practice on the 
part of employer in engaging employees as casual or temporary employees for long period without giving 
them the status and privileges of permanent employees as is held by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case 
of Umrala Gram Paychayat Vs. The Secretary, Municipal Employees Union, arising out of Civil Appeal 


9०.3209-3270/20/5, dated 22.03. 20/5, in which the order of Tribunal for regularization of Safai workers 
has been upheld by the Hon’ble Supreme Court. The Hon’ble Supreme Court in case of Narendra Kumar 
Tiwari_& others versus State of Jharkhand & others, civil appeal nos.7423-7429 of 20/8 (arising out of 


S.L.P. (Civil) १०७. /9832-798636 of 20/ 2), has held that the Regularization Rules must be given pragmative 
interpretation and order for regularization for those employees who has rendered service of !0 years or 
more from the date of the promulgation of the Regularization Rules unless there is same valid objection to 
their regularization like misconduct etc. Claimants/workmen are rendering their services for more than |5 
years as contract workers uninterruptedly without regularization which amounts unfair labour practice of 
the Act. 


84. It is added here that Hon'ble Supreme Court in latest two judgments Jaggo versus Union of India 
(supra) and Dharm Singh and others (supra) has deprecated the practice of outsourcing to shield to 
perpetuate precariousness and to sidestep fair engagement practices, where the work is inherently perennial 
and has also pointed out how Uma Devi case (supra) is not applicable to such employees, who are working 


for a long period as part time workers/daily wagers. In Jaggo versus Union of India (supra) Hon'ble 
Supreme Court has held as under:- 


l0.Appellants long and uninterrupted service, for periods extending well beyond ten year, cannot be 
brushed aside merely by labeling their initial appointment as contractual. The essence of their employment 
must be considered in the light of their sustained contribution, the integral nature of their work, and the 
fact that no evidence suggests their entry was through any illegal or surreptitious route. 


I2.Despite being labeled as “part time workers”, the appellants performed these essential tasks on a daily 
and continuous basis over extensive periods, ranging from over a decade to nearly two decades. Their 
engagement was not sporadic or temporary in nature; instead, it was recurrent, regular and akin to the 
responsibilities typically associated with sanctioned posts. Moreover, the respondents did not engage any 
other personnels for these tasks during the appellants’ entire tenure, underscoring the indispensable 
nature of their work. 


20. It is well established that the decision in Uma Devi (supra) does not intend to penalize employees who 
have rendered long years of service fulfilling ongoing and necessary functions of the State or its 
instrumentalities. The said judgment sought to prevent backdoor entries and illegal appointments that 
circumvent constitutional requirements. However, where appointments were not illegal but possibly 
"irregular," and where employees had served continuously against the backdrop of sanctioned functions 
for a considerable period, the need for a fair and humane resolution becomes paramount. Prolonged, 
continuous, and unblemished service performing tasks inherently required on a regular basis can, over the

time, transform what was initially ad-hoc or temporary into a scenario demanding fair regularization. In a 
recent judgment of this Court in Vinod Kumar and Ors. etc. Vs. Union of India & Ors. 


5. It was held that procedural formalities cannot be used to deny regularization of service to an employee 
whose appointment was termed "temporary” but has performed the same duties as performed by the 
regular employee over a considerable period in the capacity of the regular employee. The relevant paras of 
this judgment have been reproduced below: 


"6. The application of the judgment in Uma Devi (supra) by the High Court does not fit squarely with the 

facts at hand, given the specific circumstances under which the appellants were employed and have 
continued their service. The reliance on procedural formalities at the outset cannot be used to perpetually 
deny substantive rights that have accrued over a considerable period through continuous service. Their 
promotion was based on a specific notification for vacancies and a subsequent circular, followed by a 
selection process involving written tests and interviews, which distinguishes their case from the 
appointments through back door entry as discussed in the case of Uma Devi (supra). 


7. The judgment in the case Uma Devi (supra) also distinguished between "irregular" and "illegal" 
appointments underscoring the importance of considering certain appointments. 


26. While the judgment in Uma Devi (supra) sought to curtail the practice of backdoor entries and ensure 
appointments adhered to constitutional principles, it is regrettable that its principles are often 
misinterpreted or misapplied to deny legitimate claims of long-serving employees. This judgment aimed to 
distinguish between “illegal” and “irregular” appointments. It categorically held that employees in 
irregular appointments, who were engaged in duly sanctioned posts and had served continuously for more 
than ten years, should be considered for regularization as a one-time measure. However, the laudable 
intent of the judgment is being subverted when institutions rely on its dicta to indiscriminately reject the 
claims of employees, even in cases where their appointments are not illegal, but merely lack adherence to 
procedural formalities. Government departments often cite the judgment in Uma Devi (supra) to argue that 
no vested right to regularization exists for temporary employees, overlooking the judgment's explicit 
acknowledgment of cases where regularization is appropriate. This selective application distorts the 
judgment's spirit and purpose, effectively weaponizing it against employees who have rendered 
indispensable services over decades. 


85. Hon'ble Supreme Court in Dharm Singh and others (supra) has held as under: 


44.#क॥शकाठार, it must be clarified that the reliance placed by the High Court on Umadevi (Supra) to non 
suit the appellants is misplaced. Unlike Umadevi (Supra), the challenge before us is not an invitation to 
bypass the constitutional scheme of public employment. It is a challenge to the State’s arbitrary refusals to 
sanction posts despite the employer’s own acknowledgement of need and decades of continuous reliance 
on the very workforce. On the other hand, Umadevi (Supra) draws a distinction between illegal 
appointments and irregular engagements and does not endorse the perpetuation of precarious employment 
where the work itself is permanent and the State has failed, for years, to put its house in order. Recent 
decisions of this Court in Jaggo v. Union of India4 and in Shripal & Another v. Nagar Nigam, Ghaziabad5 
have emphatically cautioned that Umadevi (Supra) cannot be deployed as a shield to justify exploitation 
through long-term “ad hocism”, the use of outsourcing as a proxy, or the denial of basicparity where 
identical duties are exacted over extended periods. The principles articulated therein apply with full force 
to the present case..... 


43.46 we have observed in both Jaggo (Supra) and Shripal (Supra), outsourcing cannot become a 
convenient shield to perpetuate precariousness and to sidestep fair engagement practices where the work 
is inherently perennial. The Commission’s further contention that the appellants are not “full-time” 
employees but continue only by virtue of interim orders also does not advance their case. That interim 
protection was granted precisely because of the long history of engagement and the pendency of the 
challenge to the State’s refusals. It neither creates rights that did not exist nor erases entitlements that may 
arise upon a proper adjudication of the legality of those refusals. 


I7.Before concluding, we think it necessary to recall that the State (here referring to both the 
Union and the State governments) is not a mere market participant but a constitutional employer. It cannot 
balance budgets on the backs of those who perform the most basic and recurring public functions. Where 
work recurs day after day and year after year, the establishment must reflect that reality in its sanctioned 
strength and engagement practices. The long-term extraction of regular labour under temporary labels

corrodes confidence in public administration and offends the promise of equal protection. Financial 
stringency certainly has a place in public policy, but it 77 Civil Appeal No. 8558 of 2076 is not a talisman 
that overrides fairness, reason and the duty to organise work on lawful lines 


20. We have framed these directions comprehensively because, case after case, orders of this 
Court in such matters have been met with fresh technicalities, rolling “reconsiderations,”’ and 
administrative drift which further prolongs the insecurity for those who have already laboured for years on 
daily wages. Therefore, we have learned that Justice in such cases cannot rest on simpliciter directions, 
but it demands imposition of clear duties, fixed timelines, and verifiable compliance. As a constitutional 
employer, the State is held to a higher standard and therefore it must organise its perennial workers on a 
sanctioned footing, create a budget for lawful engagement, and implement judicial directions in letter and 
spirit. Delay to follow these obligations is not mere negligence but rather it is a conscious method of denial 
that erodes livelihoods and dignity for these workers. The operative scheme we have set here comprising of 
creation of supernumerary posts, full regularization, subsequent financial benefits, and a sworn affidavit of 
compliance, is therefore a pathway designed to convert rights into outcomes and to reaffirm that fairness 
in engagement and transparency in administration are not matters of 27 Civil Appeal No. 8558 of 2076 
grace, but obligations under Articles /4, /6 and 27 of the Constitution of India.”

The very nature of an industrial dispute as distinguished from an individual dispute, is to obtain new 
industrial conditions, not merely for the specific individuals then working form the specific individuals then 
employing them, and not for the moment only, but for the class of employees from the class of employer.... 
It is a battled by the claimants nor for themselves alone.” Section 76 of the Act supports the aforesaid

No. 10-4/2026-U.3(A)—Whereas, Malla Reddy (MR), Deemed to be University, Telangana submitted an online 
application on the UGC Portal for establishment of an off-campus centre at Krishnapuram Village, Renigunta Mandal, Tirupathi 
as per the UGC (Institutions deemed to be Universities) Regulations, 2023. 


2. And whereas, UGC, vide its letter No. 41-5/2026 (CPP-I/DU) dated 12.05.2026, informed that the application was 
examined through its Standing Committee. The Committee, after presentation of the Institution and based on the documents 
submitted, recommended for issuance of Letter of Intent (Lol) to Malla Reddy (MR), Telangana for fulfilment of certain 
conditions. 

3. And whereas, the Ministry, on advice of UGC, issued letter of Intent (Lol) dated 01.06.2026 to Malla Reddy (MR), 
Deemed to be University, Telangana for fulfilment of certain conditions within a period of three years before establishment of 
an off-campus centre at Krishnapuram village, Renigunta Mandal, Tirupathi. 

4. And further whereas, the Registrar, Malla Reddy (MR), Telangana, vide letter dated 02.06.2026, submitted the 
compliance report in respect of the conditions stipulated in the Lol. The same was forwarded to UGC for verification and 
further advice. Further, UGC, vide letter dated 03.07.2026, informed that the compliance report was accepted by the Standing 
Committee. 

5. Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred under Section 3 of the UGC Act, 1956, the Ministry of 
Education, on the advice of UGC, hereby accords approval to Malla Reddy (MR), an Institution deemed to be University, 
Telangana to start an off-campus Centre at No. 6, Krishnapuram village, Renigunta Mandal, Tirupathi. 

6. All other conditions mentioned in the earlier Notification(s) of this Ministry as well as the Rules / Regulations of 
UGC and other Statutory Councils, issued from time to time, shall continue to be adhered by Malla Reddy (MR), Deemed to 
be University, Telangana.
